cards.title: Atomic Structure: The Nucleus: Vocabulary
cards.front: What does atomic number Z count?
cards.back: Atomic number Z counts the number of protons in the nucleus; in a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons.
facts: An atom has a dense positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons at a comparatively large distance.
The nucleus contains positively charged protons and neutral neutrons; a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom but contains essentially all of the atom's mass.
Atomic number Z counts protons; mass number A counts protons plus neutrons.
Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers because they contain different numbers of neutrons.

cards.title: Atomic Structure: Orbitals: Vocabulary
cards.front: In quantum terms, what is an orbital?
cards.back: An orbital is a wave function used to describe the region where an electron is likely to be found.
facts: A wave function, or orbital, describes where an electron is likely to be found around a nucleus.
The square of the wave function corresponds to electron probability density.
Orbitals are often drawn as regions containing most of the electron probability rather than as hard-edged objects.
An s orbital is spherical; a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped; most d orbitals are four-lobed.
Electron shells increase in size and energy as they get farther from the nucleus.

cards.title: Atomic Structure: Electron Configurations: Vocabulary
cards.front: What is a ground-state electron configuration?
cards.back: It is the lowest-energy arrangement of an atom's electrons among available orbitals.
facts: A ground-state electron configuration lists the occupied orbitals for the lowest-energy arrangement of an atom's electrons.
The Aufbau principle says electrons fill lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals.
The Pauli exclusion principle says an orbital can hold two electrons only if their spins are opposite.
Hund's rule says equal-energy empty orbitals receive one electron each with parallel spins before pairing begins.
Orbital superscripts indicate how many electrons occupy that orbital or subshell.

molecule.name: sp3 Hybrid Orbitals and the Structure of Ethane: Fact-Recall

facts: Ethane is the simplest molecule containing a carbon-carbon bond.
The C-C bond in ethane forms by head-on overlap of an sp3 hybrid orbital from each carbon.
The remaining three sp3 orbitals on each carbon overlap with hydrogen 1s orbitals to make six C-H sigma bonds.
Ethane bond angles are near the tetrahedral value of 109.5 degrees.
The ethane C-C single bond is about 153 pm long and about 377 kJ/mol strong.

cards.front: What is a condensed structure?
cards.back: A shorthand structure where many C-H and C-C single bonds are not drawn but are implied by groups such as CH3, CH2, and CH.
facts: A line between atoms represents the two electrons in a covalent bond.
Condensed structures omit many C-H and C-C single bond lines; groups such as CH3, CH2, and CH imply how many hydrogens are attached.
Parentheses can group repeated substituents, as in (CH3)2 attached to one atom.
In skeletal structures, carbon atoms are normally implied at every line end and line intersection.
Hydrogens bonded to carbon are normally omitted in skeletal structures and supplied mentally to give carbon valence 4.

cards.title: dispersion forces: Concept
cards.front: What causes dispersion forces?

back.core: Momentary uneven electron distributions create temporary dipoles that induce complementary dipoles in neighboring molecules.
back.scope: They occur between all neighboring molecules, including nonpolar molecules.
back.importance: Cumulative dispersion can make larger nonpolar molecules liquids or solids.

cards.title: Chloromethane Polarity And sp3 Geometry
cards.front: In chloromethane, which atom carries δ−, which atom carries δ+, and why is the molecule polar?
cards.back: Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so Cl is δ− and the carbon bonded to Cl is δ+. The C-Cl bond dipole is not canceled by the C-H bonds, so chloromethane has a net molecular dipole toward chlorine.
facts: Electronegativity increases from left to right across a row and generally decreases down a group.
A bond dipole points toward the more electronegative atom.
Partial negative charge, δ−, appears on the more electronegative end of a polar bond.
Carbon is less electronegative than chlorine, so the C-Cl bond is polarized Cδ+-Clδ−.
The C-Cl sigma bond can be pictured as overlap between a carbon sp3 orbital and a chlorine valence orbital along the internuclear axis.
A molecule can contain polar bonds but have no net dipole if the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.

facts: A functional group is a recurring atom pattern inside a molecule that largely determines a family of chemical behavior.
Molecules with the same functional group often react in related ways even when the rest of the molecule is very different.
Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond; alkynes contain a carbon-carbon triple bond; arenes contain aromatic carbon-carbon bonding in a ring.

cards.title: Properties of Alkanes: Property Trend
cards.front: Which should boil higher: pentane or octane?
cards.back: Octane, because the larger molecule has stronger dispersion forces.
facts: Alkanes are often chemically inert toward many laboratory reagents and are sometimes called paraffins.
Alkanes can burn in oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water while releasing substantial heat.
Methane can undergo chlorine substitution under ultraviolet light to give chlorinated methane products.
Straight-chain alkane boiling and melting points generally rise as carbon count and molecular weight rise because dispersion forces increase.
More highly branched alkane isomers usually boil lower than less branched isomers because compact shapes have less surface contact and weaker dispersion attractions.

facts: Stereochemistry studies the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in molecules.
Rotation around an open-chain carbon-carbon sigma bond is possible because sigma bonds are cylindrically symmetric.
Conformations are different spatial arrangements produced by rotation around single bonds; conformers often interconvert rapidly.
A sawhorse representation views a C-C bond at an oblique angle; a Newman projection views directly down the C-C bond axis.

cards.title: Naming Cycloalkanes: Definition
cards.front: What is the general formula for a simple cycloalkane?
cards.back: CnH2n, because the saturated ring is built from CH2 units.
facts: Cycloalkanes are saturated cyclic hydrocarbons. A simple cycloalkane ring is made from CH2 units and has the general formula CnH2n.

The ring is usually the parent when it has at least as many carbons as any attached alkyl group. If a substituent chain has more carbons than the ring, the ring is named as a cycloalkyl substituent on an alkane parent.

Number a substituted cycloalkane to give the first point of difference the lowest possible locant. Choose an attachment carbon as C1, then number around the ring to minimize the locants for the remaining substituents.
Alphabetical order breaks ties when different substituents can receive the same locant set. Ignore multiplicative prefixes such as di- and tri- when applying alphabetical priority.
Halogen substituents are numbered like alkyl substituents in cycloalkane names. A bromo, chloro, fluoro, or iodo group participates in the same lowest-locant and alphabetical tie-break rules.

cards.title: Stability of Cycloalkanes: Ring Strain: Comparison
cards.front: What are the three main contributors to cycloalkane strain?
cards.back: Angle strain, torsional strain, and steric strain.
facts: Ring strain is extra molecular energy relative to a strain-free reference. Cycloalkane strain can be estimated from heats of combustion per CH2 unit.
Higher heat of combustion indicates a higher-energy molecule. A strained molecule releases more heat when completely burned.
Angle strain comes from bond angles being compressed or expanded away from the tetrahedral value. The ideal sp3 angle is about 109.5 degrees.
Torsional strain comes from eclipsing interactions between bonds on adjacent atoms. Eclipsed C-H bonds in small rings are a major torsional strain source.
Steric strain comes from nonbonded atoms or groups approaching too closely. Steric effects become important in conformational comparisons and medium rings.

cards.title: Conformations of Cycloalkanes: Concept
cards.front: Why is cyclopropane so strained?
cards.back: It has severe angle strain from 60 degree ring angles plus torsional strain from eclipsed C-H bonds.
facts: Cyclopropane is highly strained because its C-C-C angles are about 60 degrees. It also has eclipsed neighboring C-H bonds.
Cyclopropane uses bent bonds. The bonding orbitals overlap at an angle rather than pointing directly at one another, making the C-C bonds weaker than normal alkane C-C bonds.
Cyclobutane puckers slightly. Puckering increases angle strain somewhat but reduces torsional strain enough to lower the overall energy.
Cyclopentane puckers to relieve torsional strain. A common description has four carbons near one plane and the fifth carbon out of plane, so most neighboring C-H bonds are nearly staggered.
Cyclopropane and cyclobutane have similar total strain energies. The chapter gives about 115 kJ/mol for cyclopropane and about 110 kJ/mol for cyclobutane.

cards.title: Conformations of Cycloalkanes: Concept
cards.front: Why is cyclobutane slightly folded instead of perfectly square and flat?
cards.back: Folding trades a little extra angle strain for less torsional strain.
facts: Cyclopropane is highly strained because its C-C-C angles are about 60 degrees. It also has eclipsed neighboring C-H bonds.
Cyclopropane uses bent bonds. The bonding orbitals overlap at an angle rather than pointing directly at one another, making the C-C bonds weaker than normal alkane C-C bonds.
Cyclobutane puckers slightly. Puckering increases angle strain somewhat but reduces torsional strain enough to lower the overall energy.
Cyclopentane puckers to relieve torsional strain. A common description has four carbons near one plane and the fifth carbon out of plane, so most neighboring C-H bonds are nearly staggered.
Cyclopropane and cyclobutane have similar total strain energies. The chapter gives about 115 kJ/mol for cyclopropane and about 110 kJ/mol for cyclobutane.

cards.title: Conformations of Cyclohexane: Definition
cards.front: What is the chair conformation of cyclohexane?
cards.back: A puckered six-membered ring conformation with near-tetrahedral bond angles and staggered neighboring C-H bonds.
facts: Cyclohexane adopts a chair conformation that is essentially strain-free. Its C-C-C angles are close to tetrahedral and neighboring C-H bonds are staggered.

Chair cyclohexane can be drawn from two parallel offset bonds plus one carbon above and one carbon below. The upper and lower end bonds are parallel, and the lower front bond is often emphasized to show perspective.
The twist-boat conformation is higher in energy than the chair. It is nearly free of angle strain but has torsional and steric strain; the chapter gives about 23 kJ/mol above the chair.
Chair cyclohexane is the preferred baseline for conformational analysis of substituted cyclohexanes. Substituent stability is usually evaluated by comparing chair forms.

cards.title: Axial and Equatorial Bonds in Cyclohexane: Definition
cards.topic: Axial and Equatorial Bonds in Cyclohexane
cards.front: What is an axial position in chair cyclohexane?
cards.back: A position parallel to the ring axis, pointing alternately up or down around the ring.
facts: Every carbon in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial bond. Axial and equatorial positions alternate around the top and bottom faces of the chair.
Axial bonds are parallel to the ring axis. They point alternately up and down around the cyclohexane chair.
Equatorial bonds lie around the rough equator of the ring. Each equatorial bond points outward from the ring and is neither purely vertical nor parallel to the ring axis.
Cis/trans and axial/equatorial answer different questions. Cis/trans describes same face versus opposite face; axial/equatorial describes conformation-specific bond direction.
A ring flip exchanges axial and equatorial positions. After a ring flip, axial substituents become equatorial and equatorial substituents become axial.

cards.title: Conformations of Monosubstituted Cyclohexanes: Concept
cards.front: Which conformation is usually more stable for a monosubstituted cyclohexane: axial or equatorial?
cards.back: Equatorial, because it avoids the main 1,3-diaxial steric contacts caused by axial placement.
facts: A monosubstituted cyclohexane is usually more stable with the substituent equatorial. The axial conformation places the substituent near axial hydrogens on carbons three atoms away.
Axial substituents create 1,3-diaxial interactions. For axial methylcyclohexane, the methyl group interacts with two axial hydrogens on the same side of the ring.
The axial penalty for methylcyclohexane is about 7.6 kJ/mol. This corresponds to two gauche-butane-like interactions of about 3.8 kJ/mol each.
About 95 percent of methylcyclohexane molecules have the methyl group equatorial at room temperature. The lower-energy equatorial conformation dominates the equilibrium.
Larger substituents have larger axial penalties. The chapter's table lists small penalties for CN and halogens, moderate penalties for methyl and ethyl, and a large penalty for tert-butyl.

cards.title: Conformations of Polycyclic Molecules: Definition
cards.front: What is a polycyclic molecule?
cards.back: A molecule containing two or more rings.
facts: A polycyclic molecule contains two or more rings. Fused rings share a bond and the two atoms at that bond are bridgehead atoms.
Decalin consists of two fused cyclohexane rings. It can exist as cis-decalin or trans-decalin depending on the relationship of the bridgehead hydrogens.
Cis-decalin has bridgehead hydrogens on the same face of the fused ring system. Trans-decalin has the bridgehead hydrogens on opposite faces.
Steroids contain fused ring systems that can be analyzed using cyclohexane conformational principles. The same cis/trans fusion and chair-substituent ideas apply to larger fused-ring frameworks.
Norbornane is bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane. The name encodes seven total carbons and three bridges of 2, 2, and 1 carbon between the bridgeheads.

cards.front: What does bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane mean for norbornane?
cards.back: It is a seven-carbon bicyclic molecule with three bridges containing 2, 2, and 1 carbons between the bridgeheads.
facts: A polycyclic molecule contains two or more rings. Fused rings share a bond and the two atoms at that bond are bridgehead atoms.
Decalin consists of two fused cyclohexane rings. It can exist as cis-decalin or trans-decalin depending on the relationship of the bridgehead hydrogens.
Cis-decalin has bridgehead hydrogens on the same face of the fused ring system. Trans-decalin has the bridgehead hydrogens on opposite faces.
Steroids contain fused ring systems that can be analyzed using cyclohexane conformational principles. The same cis/trans fusion and chair-substituent ideas apply to larger fused-ring frameworks.
Norbornane is bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane. The name encodes seven total carbons and three bridges of 2, 2, and 1 carbon between the bridgeheads.
